children: Iron ore prices slid for a sixth straight session on Wednesday to a near one-month low, as some major steelmakers in top consumer China pledged to control production to lower steel inventory amid rapidly falling margins.
By 0203 GMT, the most-traded iron ore contract on China's Dalian Commodity Exchange (DCE)
dipped 0.28% to 706 yuan ($105.18) a metric ton, its weakest since August 21.
The benchmark October iron ore (SZZFV6) on the Singapore Exchange was 0.2% lower at $95.25 a ton, as of 0153 GMT. It earlier hit a low of $95.05, the lowest since August 20.

The state-backed China Iron and Steel Association (CISA), along with 45 major steelmakers including China Baowu Steel Group, called on domestic steelmakers across the industry to firmly implement production controls to lower elevated steel inventory, according to a statement on its WeChat account on Tuesday.

"The steel industry has been facing strong supply, weak demand, depressed prices and shrinking profitability since early this year, piling up mounting pressure on steelmakers...while the problem stems from falling demand, the fundamental solution to navigate through the challenges lies in the supply side," the steel association said.
Analysts said that weighed on demand prospects for steelmaking ingredients, putting prices under pressure.
Profitability among Chinese steelmakers weakened sharply, hit by elevated production costs and sluggish steel demand.

Steel benchmarks on the Shanghai Futures Exchange were mixed. Rebar
